HUGHES (Victoria).,,SUPPLY-GOVERNMENT TARIFF POLICY.,,,Were it not that hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House have endeavoured to show that the farmers of Canada are not in favour of the protective policy advocated by the Conservative party, I should not have risen to address the House to-night. After the last election in North Ontario the Liberals tried to make out that that election was won by them because the farmers had prouounced against protection. Some of these hon. gentlemen had even the hardihood to advance that same argument in the House. Let me compare the result in the last by-election in North Ontario with the result in the by-election a few years ago when Mr. McLeod defeated the sitting Liberal member, Mr. Duncan Graham, and that comparison will illustrate the actual condition of affairs. In the large agricultural township of Brock, the Hon. Geo. E. Foster polled 592 votes as against 581 polled by Mr. McLeod in that previous election and 336 polled by Mr. Grant in the last election and 437 polled by Mr. Duncan Graham. I refer now to the two by-elections which were engineered by the Minister of Labour or the Postmaster General or in whatever capacity he went to the riding. In the recent by-election the village of Cannington polled 115 votes for Mr. Foster, while it polled 138 for Mr. Augus McLeod in 1897, Mr. Grant's vote being increased from 104 for Mr. Graham to 157. I will not enter into an explanation as to the change of votes in that village where there are hardly any farmers, but that explanation will be given in the proper time and place. The tine agricultural township of Scott gave Mr. Foster a majority of seven while in the by-election that Mr. McLeod ran in, it gave the Liberal candidate a majority ol' twenty-one. In the agricultural township of Scott the Liberal-Conservatives gained in the last election. In the township of Thorah which adjoins Beaverton and along which there are some government works, the Conservative majority fell off, and that was the only agricultural part of the riding where it did fall off. Beaverton gave Mr. Foster only ninety-six votes, whereas is gave Mr. McLeod 108 votes, and Mr. Grant received ninety-nine as against seventy for Mr. Graham. The agricultural township of Mara polled 190 votes for Mr. Foster and only 172 for Mr. McLeod in the previous election. There again we find that in an agricultural township the farmers increased their votes for protection. When we come to the township of Rama where are situated the wood alcohol works of the company with which the government is associated, Mr. Foster polled eighty-one votes as against 118 for Mr. McLeod, showing a large falling off. In as much as the Liberals have gone around the country saying that this was a vote against protection I will quote from a few speeches delivered to the horny-handed sons of toil on that occasion as reported in the ' Globe ' of March 3. Mr. Wm. Thompson, a manufacturer at Longford and Orillia, a very esteemed young gentleman said :

The Standard Chemical Works employ twice the men they informed the government they would employ at the time the government agreed to assist the company in the disposal of a portion of their output. He explained how the money of the company is distributed through the district for wood, teaming, and wages.
That had nothing to dj with the money distributed in the election.
During the last year there had been more mortgages paid off in Muskoka than in any previous year.'

That is no doubt due to the fact that the government pays an enormous price for this wood alcohol which is sold in the United States at a far cheaper rate, and which Should be sold in Canada cheaper than ever before, because of the market that has grown up for the by-products of wood alcohol. As to the teams employed by this company, forty or fifty of them turned out to draw votes for the Liberal candidate, all of which was paid for by the people of the Dominion in the extra price which the government gives for this wood alcohol. Then we find Mr. Tudhope, a member of the local house, a very estimable gentleman, speaking thus :

In answer to the suggestion that had been made, that he was supporting the Liberal government because the government had increased the duty on buggies to 35 per cent, Mr. Tudhope explained that that duty is now really $17.50 as against $25 under the national policy. Deducting the duty on the raw material assembled by the carriage-builder, his protection really came to only 7 per cent or 8 per cent.

And yet this gentleman has grown rich by the sale of his buggies to the farmers of the Dominion of Canada, under a protection to the tune of thirty-five per cent. Mr. Tudhope's father was an honest and industrious carriage maker in the town of Orillia, and he grew rich under the national policy by selling wagons and buggies to the farmers of the counties of Simcoe and Ontario. He was a good Conservative, but his son deserted the Liberal Conservative cause, owing to the wily influence of some member of the Liberal party in inducing him to make a deal for the supply of wood alcohol to the Dominion government, and Mr. Tudhope stumped the country and used his influence on behalf of the Liberal candidate. And then these gentlemen boast that the solid farmer vote of North Ontario defeated Mr. Foster. Then we come to a speech de-
livered on that occasion by Mr. Peuclien, who said.:

He wanted a little help and went to Ottawa, thinking that as an old Conservative he would have little difficulty in his lobbying. He found it impossible to even see several of the ministers on whom he called, and he came away quite disheartened. After the change of government he went down again. He had no difficulty in seeing the ministers, received a fair and businesslike hearing, and he found that when the ministers were shown a reasonable proposition, and one that was likely to be a benefit to the country
and I presume incidentally to the gentleman concerned

-they would assist it. Assistance was promised him, and the result was the establishment of his business in five Canadian towns, and the expenditure of several millions of dollars. He did not know that the industry would have been started if there had not been a change of government.

All these speeches, you will notice, are appeals to the horny-handed sons of toil. On that occasion the Postmaster General, the Minister of Labour, Sir William Mulock, was present, and he appealed to the farmers. Did he point out where they were ground down under the iron heel of any monopoly Did he show where one cent was unfairly taken from them, directly or indirectly by the manufacturers ? No; but he quoted a little doggerel poetry. He appealed to the lower element of his hearers, and this was his appeal :
Lives of farmers all remind us We must work at every chance,
And in working get behind us Bigger patches on our pants.

I may tell my hon. friend that he never was a farmer. In the old days in Bowman-ville, near which town I had the privilege of growing up, in a good old Grit riding, there was an old agricultural implement manufacturer named Porter; my hon. friend from Centre Toronto (Mr. Brock) will know him very well. When a farmer came into his store to buy a set of harrows or a plough, the old gentleman would commence showing him beneath the implement in order to get the farmer to stoop. If he found the farmer's trousers worn out in front and not behind, the farmer was trusted for the implement. I want to tell my hon. friend the Postmaster General that he never was a farmer, otherwise he would not have insulted the intelligence of the farmers of that locality by telling them that any respectable farmer would have his trousers worn out behind. They are worn out in front. But the hon. Postmaster General did not complete the poetry. The next stanza went thus :
But if William swells the taxes,
As he is inclined to do.
The farmers soon will have no clothing For to sew the catches to.

69776,ca.proc.d.1903-06-17.3.3.4,1903-06-17,6e709d61-48a8-4abc-ac0f-a0e806704351,ca.m.8006,Mr. L. P. DEMERS (St John and Iberville).,,SUPPLY-GOVERNMENT TARIFF POLICY.,IT, 1903",,"(Translation.) Mr. Speaker, the motion brought forward as an amendment to that of the hon. Minister of Finance is the summary of a series of articles and speeches written or delivered by its mover, the hon. member for St. Mary's (Hon. Mr. Tarte) in the course of the last ten months or so. In his speech delivered a moment ngo, the hon. member entreated the members on this side of the House to hear his appeal, to listen to the plea he was about to make.

On the whole, I do not think this new proposal made by the hon. member has much chance of winning favour either in this House or in the province of Quebec. That tariff issue, it seems to me, has been well threshed out for many years back. I do not know that there is in the province of Quebec a free trade party. The hon. member compared free trade and protection; but I repeat it, I do not know that there is in this country a party favouring free trade pure and simple. People's ideas are settled in this respect and they are in the moderate vein.

I do not think the electors will take kindly to the arguments set forth by the hon. member for St. Mary's, and that for several reasons. In the first place we read in the gospel to beware of false prophets ; and while, on the one hand, we have the hon. member's utterances for the last ten months in favour of protection, on the other hand, we have his numerous protests for ten years in the opposite sense. Which are we to believe ? To his statements of to-day we can oppose the statements of the member for L'lslet, of the candidate in Beauharnois, of the ex-Minister of Public Works and of the candidate in St. Mary's division of Montreal during the last contest.
Those who know the hon. member cannot fail to have strong objections to following him in the path into which he would fain lead away the people.
In the first place, I notice that instead 154J

of seeking commercial reciprocity with the United States, he believes to-day in increasing the customs duties. That is an entirely new departure, as I shall show. The hon. member for St. Mary's came out, in 1893, as Liberal candidate in the county of L'lslet, and was elected. Here is the programme he submitted to the electors of that county. 1 find it quoted on page 1019 of * Hansard,' for 1893, as follows

I am resolved to turn all my efforts towards obtaining changes in the tariff, such, as to permit tbe agricultural class to buy cheaply the things they need, and to sell dearer the produce of the soli.

The manufacturers in the large cities who realize hundreds of thousands of dollars profit per year, by means of the present tariff oppose these reforms. They are organized into an association. and without party distinctions they support the government, the policy of which builds their fortune. From their point of view they are right. The so-called national policy, adopted in 1879, with the object of favouring the establishment and development of our industries in preventing foreign products from entering Canada, has not to-day the same raison d'etre.

The interests of the manufacturers have been protected long enough. The hour has come for protecting the interests of agriculture. The manufacturers' interest is to keep the Canadian market closed against the manufactured products of the United States, in order to sell their own goods at higher prices.
The interest of the Canadian farmer is to work towards having the American market opened to him. in order to sell dearer his produce.
Further on, he added :
Let us see that the American market which is practically closed against us, be opened to us, so that we may sell there, our horses, our potatoes. our eggs, fowls, &c.
The Canadian farmer will find in that a double interest. First, he will pay less for what he needs, and he will sell his produce to better advantage.

The struggle is then really between the farmer, who needs the American market and the manufacturer who is afraid to make less profits if the American manufacturer can come and compete with him for the sale of furniture, farming implements, cotton fabrics, vehicles, &c.
Following up the same idea, the hon. member said :
Who does not remember, Mr. Speaker, the by-campaigns that we fought, for instance, that of Drummond and Arthabaska, In 1877 ? It is one of the contests I regret the most, be it said by the way.
That is not quite in line with his Chatham speech of 1902 :

Well, we carried those by-elections, and the general elections by saying : Let us adopt a protective tariff, and we will force the American government to treat with us. The illusion we had then must have vanished to-day ; but it has nevertheless served to carry the elections of 1891.
This was going on in 1893. In 1896, the hon. member, then a candidate for the Liberal party in the county of Beauharnois, sent out to the electors of that constitu-

ency a lengthy circular, of which I hold a copy, wherein he expressed his persistent belief that an increase of the duties would be a misfortune for the country; and that our endeavour should be to secure reciprocity with the United States. He said :
For eighteen years, the Tory party has been in power.
Notice, ' The Tory party.'

What have been the results of their administration. I am not one of those who say that everything the Conservative party have done is wrong. If I were to say so, I would be casting blame upon myself, for, up to 1891, I have followed in the ranks of that party, though at times, on certain points, at variance with its policy. But, I have no hesitation in saying that the purpose we had in view in 1S78, when the protective system was adopted, has not been attained.

Our favourite argument during the electoral contest of 1878, was that, by increasing the customs duties, we would force the United States to grant us a treaty of commercial reciprocity. Far from seeing our expectations materialize, we have from that date got to loggerheads with our neighbours, who maintained their tariff and even at times modified it in such a way as to do us the greatest harm.
So that in this respect, the hon. member has greatly varied from the opinions he held in 1893 and in 1896.

Now, in that hon. gentleman's opinion, what was in 1896 the position held, the part played by manufacturers in this country 1 His contention was that they preyed on the people ; that they were monopolists, and underpaid their men. He claimed, besides, that the farmers were being ruined. In that same speech delivered in this House, February 21, 1893, at page 1026 of ' Hansard,' he said :

There is no doubt that, thanks to protection, a certain number of manufacturers have built up large fortunes, but there is no doubt either that the public fortune is not equitably divided. In Montreal we see men who, poor in 1878, have become millionaires. We see at the same time the rural districts losing their population.

So, the country was being depopulated in 1893; had the financial condition of the farmers improved in 1896 ? Well, let us see what he said in this connection in his address to the electors of Beauharnois :
I need not say that the abolition, or at least the reduction, of the duties would be a clear gain to the farmers, and would increase in a large measure our trade with the United States.
And further on :

Then, again, by allowing the free importation into our country of certain manufactured goods, we will enable consumers to get at a lower price the goods which they need. For eighteen years past large manufacturers have enjoyed a measure of protection which is now found to be excessive. The time has come, it seems to me, for the farmer and the consumer to have their innings.
So, that the consumer and the farmer had not yet had their innings; only manu-Mr. DEMERS (St. John and Iberville!.
facturers had been so favoured. Referring to the latter in that same manifesto, he said :

Mr. Laurier and his friends have no thought of destroying manufactures. Why would they do so ? They only wish that manufacturers should make fair profits and no more. By allowing the importation free or at reduced rates of the raw material used in industries, we shall ensure to manufactures advantages which will enable them to sell their products cheaper than they do now. Iron, coal oil and many other articles of raw material should enter our country without having to pay the heavy duties to which they are subjected to-day for the benefit of a few score of individuals. Of course, monopolists, those who make every year hundreds of thousands of dollars at the expense of the consumer, are strongly opposed to any change. They are going to make a supreme effort in the present contest, as they know Mr. Laurier will govern Canada in the interest of the people, and not In their own, as the present government is doing.
That able candidate puts the question : ' Is the government the friend of the farmer and the workingman ? ' to which he gives the following reply :

A fiscal policy which obliges consumers to pay a tribute of from 25 to 30 per cent to a privileged class, cannot be favourable to the masses. Farmers realize what their position is. A couple of years more like those we have gone through and agriculture in this country will be ruined.
Another prophecy ! So much for the workers in the country ; now, for those in cities :

Inquire from workingmen in cities what is their present condition. They do not find work half the year long ; and they are paid salaries barely sufficient to keep their families from suffering from hunger. Never has there been so much misery in the city of Montreal as during the year which has just elapsed. The same is true of all large cities. The reason for that state of things is very plain. Monopolists
Monopolists once more

-having done away with all the small factories. have now full control of the labour market. They pay to the workingman whatever wages they please. See what is going on at Valleyfleld, where a great number of robust, honest, hard-working men do not earn more than 90 cents per day. The average wage paid in that large factory does not exceed 55 cents per day.

Such was the appeal made in 1896 to th,e electors of Beauharnois by that hon. gentleman, then a candidate in that constituency. In the newspaper ' Le Cultivateur,' in 1896, the hon. member for St. Mary's published articles to the same intent. On June 13. 1896, under the heading ' Down with tributes,' I read the following:
A few years more of our fiscal system will cause our working classes to fall into a state of bondage similar to that in which monopolists in the United States have long held their employees.
J|
Let us free ourselves from the grasp of monopolists.
On June 6, 1896, I find In the same paper :

We wish manufacturers to make reasonable profits. But it seems to us the time has come for workingmen and consumers to have their day. It is time we should cease paying tribute to men such as Mr. Simps ji and scores of others of his stamp.

The electorate followed the advice of ' Le Cultivateur.' The Liberal party came into power, and a moderate tariff favourable to manufacturing, industries inasmuch as it enables them to realize legitimate profits, was adopted. The people put their trust in the Liberal party ; they confided in the latter's promises, and the hon. member for St. Mary's was asked to enter the cabinet. Let us see what he thought of the Fielding tariff on April 24, 1897. I read the following in a letter from Ottawa which appeared in his paper, ' Le Cultivateur,' and which I take to have been written by him, as the tone betrays its author :
It is in order, it is a matter of necessity, rather, that there should be a few groans here and there, on the part of those who favour monopolists. .
Monopolies once more
-who, under the old regime, -were the real holders of power.
Further on:
It is fair, therefore, to restore equality between the manufacturer, the merchant, the consumer.
On May 1, 1897, he wrote :

Legitimate industries have no right to complain. Specific duties, which had become so obnoxious on account of the wrongful use they had been put to, are things of the past. Manufacturers who were protected by duties amounting to 30, 40, 50, 70 per cent on certain articles, should not be surprised at the changes effected. They could not expect that such an insufferable condition of things should be maintained. A margin suflieient to enable them to carry on their business has been allowed to them, but they will no longer have a monopoly.
Such were the views of the hon. gentleman expressed Inf his paper ' Le Cultivateur.'

From 1896 until the elections of 1900, Canada, under the [DOT]present administration, had increased immensely. Our trade had grown by 8150,000,000. Our exports of manufactured goods had doubled. Then, the hon. gentleman resolved to seek electiou in St. Mary's division.

I heard a moment ago the hon. member for Centre Toronto (Mr. Brock) state that members on this side of the House do not vote in accordance with the wishes of their electors. It seems to me that the first duty of a member of parliameut is to vote in accordance with the promises he made when seeking election. Let us see what statements the hon. member for St. Mary's made in October, 1900, as shown by his organ
' La Patrie,' of October 18th. It seems to be a verbatim report of the speech.

Reference will be made in the course of the contest to the revision of the tariff ; you will be told that we granted a preference to Great Britain of 33J per cent ; that is so, and it is the best thing we have done.
Farther on :
Industries-some of them, at least-were protected to an extent which we thought excessive. We slightly reduced the duties. We gave to Great Britain a preference of 33J per cent.
Farther on :

We were killing two birds with one stone. Please notice : We were lightening the burdens of the people ; we were giving an impulse to industries at the same time as reducing the duties. We were only intelligently pricking on capitalists who had been somewhat lagging behind. What was the consequence ? Canadian industries, feeling a little more the keen edge of competition, improved their methods. Manufacturers imported new machinery in order to be in a position to compete to greater advantage. The result is now apparent. We have witnessed within the two or three last years unprecedented developments. The trade of the country has increased by $150,000,000. I repeat it, if you are not satisfied, you are rather hard to satisfy.
Since Canada's trade bas not ceased increasing in the meantime, are we not entitled to say to the hon. gentleman :
you are not satisfied, you are rather hard to satisfy ?

Now here is something in regard to tariff revision, which is more surprising and which most of the hon. members are not prepared for. It is an extract from the programme of the hon. gentleman to his electors, to be found in ' La Patrie ' of October 18, 1900. It is on such representations as these that the hon. member was elected in St. Mary's division :

By our revision of the tariff we have given a new impetus to industry. For one, I believe on the stability of the tariff. I do not mean that there may not be necessity later on for some readjustments ; but the main features of the tariff should not be changed.
The hon. gentleman, as we see, was quite orthodox then. He was in favour of keeping the tariff, in its main features, as it is to-day.

Well, barely two years after making these statements, when the country was enjoying an ever-increasing prosperity, and without any change having taken place in the economic conditions of the country, the hon. member thought fit to start a movement in favour of high protection, contending that on it alone the country depended for its welfare. I think we are fairly entitled to say to him that these ten months during which he has been campaigning in favour of protection do not outweigh in our estimate his efforts for a period of ten years in the ranks of the Liberal party.
We have been told by the hon. member that petitions had been addressed to the

government, asking for changes in the tariff. But who started this agitation, if not the hon. member himself ? Who travelled the country, impressing manufacturers with the idea that they urgently needed protection, if not the . hon. member ?

Last session, when the hon. member for Laval introduced his motion demanding protection for the farmers, the hon. member for St. Mary's did not speak in the same strain as to-day. He contended in the way I do now, that an agitation had been started for the purpose of having vegetables subjected to a duty. Here are his very words :
It is very easy to create ill-feeling among people who think they do not sell their products high enough ; but that grievance can easily be remedied.

As a matter of fact, that is what happened, and the proof that no real uneasiness exists is that Liberal candidates in the last by-elections had no difficulty in securing their return by increased majorities.

The hon. member made a comparison between the conditions existing in the United States, and those existing in Great Britain, between a free trade and a protectionist country, for the purpose of showing that the working classes in the United States receive a higher remuneration for their labour than those in Great Britain. An easy answer to this is that workingmen in Germany get still lower wages than British workmen, although the German tariff is highly protective. Wages are higher in America than in Europe, where workingmen are willing to work for a pittance.

On the other hand, the welfare of our farming community is undeniable. That welfare has been so marked since the introduction of the admirable tariff to which the hon. member himself gave his approval, that our farmers, instead of quitting the country to seek employment in the United States factories, now turn to settling in the North-west. And even farmers from the United States are seen constantly crossing the line, thus adding to our numbers and our wealth.
The whole thing may be summed up as follows :

SPROULE (East Grey).,,SUPPLY-GOVERNMENT TARIFF POLICY.,IT, 1903",,"I do not rise for the purpose of confuting the logic of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Demers), because I have not the honour of understanding his language as well as my hon. friend from Saskatchewan (Mr. Davis) who seemed to enjoy the speech as much as if it were delivered in his native tongue. I understand, however, that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Demers) quoted speeches from the hon. member (Hon. Mr. Tarfe) in ""the past which are supposed to contain different sentiments from those which he has announced to-night. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Demers) could profitably employ his time by taking the speeches of seven-tenths of the members on his own side of the House delivered a few years ago, and he would find that they are diametrically opposite in sentiment from the speeches which his friends delivered to-day. The hon. gentleman forgets that conditions may change in a country, that the views of public men may change with the conditions, that what was suitable in 1896 may not be suitable at the present time, and not be suitable in the future. It is the part of wisdom that public men should change their views in order to meet the requirements of the day.

I am here to-night to support this resolution because I believe it embodies principles that are beneficial to Canada at the present time. My hon. friend (Hon. Mr. Tarte) makes this proposition at the outset:
To Insure permanency and the further progress of existing industries and to bring about the creation of new ones.
What member of this House or what true Canadian will dissent from that principle ? His next proposition is :
To inspire confidence for the investment of Canadian, British and foreign capital.
We must inspire confidence before capital will be invested, and we must create permanence so that capitalists may have a fair return on their investment. The next proposition is :
To insure to the farmer the full advantages of a prosperous home market, and to secure better wages for the labourer.

Who will say that is wrong ? The home market is the best market for our farmers. It yields the farmer the largest return for his labour, because a portion of his profits is not consumed in the charges for transporting his products to a foreign market. The next proposition in my hou. friend's resolution is.

To render impossible the slaughtering of our markets by the products of foreign countries, foreign industries, foreign combines, and foreign agricultural products, and to bring about the more rapid expansion of our vast resources.
With these objects of the resolution we must all agree.
To promote closer trade relations between the different provinces of the Dominion of Canada and between the Dominion of Canada and the n other country.

Is there an lion, gentleman on the other side, from the premier down to the lowest member, who will say that there is anything wrong in that principle ? The hon. member (Hon. Mr. Tarte) further says in his resolution :

It is the bounden and imperative duty of the government to revise and readjust, without delay, the present tariff in such a manner as to leave no doubt as to the determination of the Canadian people to adopt and maintain a fiscal policy adequately and firmly protective of the large national interest at stake. And also to carry out an energetic transportation policy which will give to our merchandise and products of all kinds commodious, quick and cheap access to the markets of our country and to those of foreign nations trading with us.

These are the aims of the resolution proposed by the hon. member for St. Mary's division of Montreal, and these are the matters to which I shall briefly direct the attention of the House. The first question that arises is :

need of a revision of the tariff at the present time ? Year after year the government have told us that the time is coming when they must revise the tariff, but year after year they have put off revision until some time in the future. Here is one reason why the tariff should be revised now. Last year we imported .$120,000,000 worth of goods from foreign countries the greater part of which could be manufactured at home, and of that, nearly $08,000,000 worth represented manufactured goods. The aim of our manufacturers is to supply the requirements of the people of Canada, and the fact that these requirements are being supplied by foreign countries indicate the necessity for a tariff revision. It is sufficient for me to know that foreign goods are coming into the tune of $08,000,000, to believe that the tariff should be revised. In view of this it must be admitted that the present tariff works to the disadvantage of the Canadian manufacturer, the Canadian farmer, the Canadian artisan, the Canadian miner, and the Canadian labourer. In. proportion as you bring in these foreign goods, to that proportion do you deprive the Canadian workman of the labour which ought be his. These important resolutions have been moved in the House to-night and the government are silent. Do they think it is not worth their while to speak, or that it is inexpedient to do so ? Do the government think that they can sit silently by and allow the interest of our industrial classes to be sacrificed without moving hand or foot to supply a remedy. It is said that this is not an opportune time for this revision. Some weeks ago the Finance Minister told us that times were prosperous and that we should not disturb the existing
K
situation. That reminds me of the logic of the old man, who, when the rain was pouring through the roof of his shanty, was asked:

69779,ca.proc.d.1903-06-17.3.3.7,1903-06-17,7b93f979-f291-49f1-9a5c-54d08800f177,ca.m.2348,Mr. SPROULE.,,SUPPLY-GOVERNMENT TARIFF POLICY.,IT, 1903",,"That is the kind of logic the government is using to-day. Do they not know that bad times follow good times, and is it not provident to provide for the bad times when there is a buoyant revenue and when a change can be made without causing any material disturbance ? When hard times come as they are sure to come, and bring about decreased values and decreased consumption, and when the slaughter goods of other countries flood the Canadian market; is it then that the government think a remedy should be applied ? Will they wait until that time comes ? If they do, they are not the provident legislators the Canadian people desire to have controlling the destinies of the country. But that is what they are doing to-day. When the products of other countries flood our markets, as they did from 1874 to 1878, and bring about hard times, the worst we have experienced in Canada, then and not until then the government are prepared to move. Is that what the Canadian people want ? I say it is not. They want the very reverse of that. Every class and every industry of the country will need protection then. Many of them need it to-day. Need I mention the fact of the large importations of agricultural products to convince this House that the farmers of this country need increased protection to-day ? Need I remind the labourer of this country that the importation of $60,000,000 of manufactured goods is taking away the labour that should be enjoyed in Canada, and giving it to Americans, English, Germans and others who are manufacturing these goods ? Need I remind the miner of British Columbia, where the mining industry is stagnant to-day for the want of protection ? Need I remind the men who are manufacturing steel in our country that their industry is on the wane to-day because it needs protection to keep it alive and moving 1 I do not think so. All these people know and see plainly that there is an urgent need to-day for a revision of the tariff. What we need for the future, in my judgment, is a higher or adequate protective tariff to protect the manufacturer of the country, the farmer of the country, the labourer of the country, the miner of the country and the artisan of the country. That, I say, is one of the needs of the situation to-day. That need is growing greater and greater every day. Will the government move before the fatal day comes, be-

fore it is too late, before capital is kept out of the country, or the capital that is employed here is lost, and before the manufacturer will be obliged to close his factory and the labourer to go out of employment ? In addition to that, we need to-day an imperial zollverein, as outlined by the Eight Hon. Joseph Chamberlain a few weeks ago. That is what we need in the Dominion of Canada and the British empire to-day; and when that is brought about, I am sure we shall have better results from it than many imagine at the present time. Along with that we require cheap and quick transportation, to lay down the products of our country in the markets in which they are sold, in the shortest possible space of time and at the cheapest possible cost. That is one of the great requisites of the time. I have just returned to-day from our north-west country. The outlook there for the future is bright and hopeful. The influx of immigration is very great. The increased acreage brought under cultivation this year is immense. The crops are looking splendid, and the farmers are assured of a good crop owing to a plentiful supply of rain up to the present time. The only fear they express is that there will be blockades in the future when their grain is ready to be moved. What are the government doing to provide for that future ? The lethargy that pervades the ranks of the government to-day is noticeable. They are dealing with odds and ends. No great national scheme has been propounded for making the highways of commerce what they should be for handling the products of the country. Where is the fast Atlantic service, which we ought to have had years ago to transport our products to the British market quickly and cheaply ? We are told that the government have received two tenders, but that they are dillydallying with the subject, as they have done for years. What are they doing for the harbours of the country ? As I passed along Lake Superior, I saw that little or nothing was being done to the harbours. There is an immediate demand for action. Are the government equal to that demand. In my opinion they are not. They are not improving our harbours to-day as they should do in preparation for the transportation of the products of the west. They are leaving this work to the future, quite regardless of the consequences. The one great fear the people in the west have is that the government are not equal to the necessities of the situation. They say that the government appear to be asleep. They ask what they are doing about the improvement of the St. Andrew's rapids, that great important work should be carried to completion at the earliest moment ? There is, comparatively speaking, nothing being done in the matter. In all these lines the government seem to be doing practically little or nothing. That is not what the people of this country expected of them. In view

of these considerations, and the hon. member for St. Mary's division, Montreal (Hon. Mr. Tarte) has propounded a policy that is admirably suited to the requirements of Canada. I am prepared to support it. I am glad to see the hon. member come out from his friends-his friends of the past. He can have the satisfaction of knowing that he disagreed with them on great national issues that are of vital importance to the people of Canada to-day. He can well afford to disagree with them on these lines. The people of Canada are at his back. Many of his late friends on that side of the House would, I am quite sure, get up and defend him but that they are ashamed to do so or to vote against the government. Judging by their speeches in the tariff debate, many of them would support the resolution he has moved, because it is on the lines these gentlemen talked. But will they do it to-night ? I challenge them to show that they have the courage of their convictions by standing by the very policy which they advocated in the budget debate a few weeks ago. I do not think they will do so; but because I believe in the policy propounded in this resolution by the hon. member for St. Mary's division, Montreal, I am prepared to give it my support and vote.

,Liberal,,Joseph Israël Tarte,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=a1231855-4bec-419e-9184-2deabd03d8a5&Language=E&Section=ALL
69783,ca.proc.d.1903-06-17.3.3.11,1903-06-17,59ffa06f-4177-4aef-8f3c-df8d6c63bf2a,ca.m.9193,Mr. BELL.,,SUPPLY-GOVERNMENT TARIFF POLICY.,IT, 1903",,"That is really the question which occupies the attention of every hon. member, and to which every hon. member would most willingly devote his attention. That being the case, it cannot he doubted that the proposition of my hon. friend from St. Mary's (Hon. Mr. Tarte) is one of the highest importance. It has to do, not only with our position to-day but with our position in the future. No one can doubt that the hon. member for St. Mary's has made a very wonderful plea for the adoption by this country of a protective policy. JVe have in Canada to-day a measure of protection, hut I think that the arguments advanced by the hon. member are exceedingly powerful and ought to convince the government that it is necessary they should take some steps in advance and decide on a fixed and determined policy. As has been pointed out by the hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Hughes) capitalists are looking to Canada as a field for investment, and it is eminently desirable that they should have the assurance that there is little or no chance of a reversal of the policy of protection, which assurance they would have if the government would accept this amendment. If you can present to the world the enormous natural advantages, the enormous fund of natural wealth which Canada specially possesses, if - you can also show that there has been adopted a policy which will guarantee to capital safe investment and sure return, we shall not have long to wait for the incoming of capital so necessary for the development of our country.

There can he no doubt at all that, so long as there is uncertainty, so long as there is a possibility of a change of course and a reversal of policy, foreign capital will look carefully before it makes investment in our country. But, with stability in that respect, with an understanding reached by the people of Canada that they looked upon protection as a wise course to follow, I am sure we should not have long to wait for the capital which, with population, is all that is required to make of Canada one of the wealthiest commonwealths in the world. The hon. member for St. Mary's division interested me very much in that portion of his speech in which he dealt with the economic history of the United States, and showed that the accumulation of wealth in that country amounts at this moment-if I understood his figures-to about $1,200 per head of the population. That wealth has

probably been created In something like a hundred years. Of course, a hundred years ago the United States had made some important beginning towards commercial advancement and national wealth, but that enormous wealth involved in the idea, of a country with 80,000,000 of people who have something like $6,000 or $7,000 per family has been created almost entirely within the last hundred years. In Canada, we have an area equal to that of the United States, resources as great and a population which, in its beginning is as promising and as well adapted to attain success in commercial pursuits. We have here wealth of every kind, and we have one particular form of wealth which will count in the immediate future. In the water powers of Canada we have wealth far surpassing anything of the same kind in the United States, an element of national wealth that will count for a great deal in the near future. Therefore, we have every condition which was possessed by the United States when they entered upon the career which they have pursued with such remarkable success up to the present time. Living beside them, separated geographic-all}7 only by an imaginery line, we find upon one side amazing advancement, enormous cities, the highest and most minute development of every form of industry. Why do we find on one side such marked advancement as to attract the attention of the whole civilized world, and, on the other side comparatively steady and, to a certain extent satisfactory, yet exceedingly slow progress as compared with the country on the other side of the international boundary ? There is only one thing that we can point to as a difference between the two countries, and that is that we in Canada have lived up to this time, and especially up to 1867, under a system of exceedingly low tariffs, not intended to develop industry, while, for nearly a hundred years, that is since 1809, the United States has been constantly and persistently pursuing a course of protection intended to develop in that country great lines of manufacturing industry. There is no other appreciable difference that I can at this moment think of that would account for the marked difference in the rate of progress between the people of the United States and the people of Canada. If we had adopted a protective system in this country ; if we had developed the older provinces of this country as quickly as we should have done under a protective system, We would have realized our destiny in the form of confederation much earlier than we did ; we would, at a much earlier day, have brought the whole northern part of America under one form of government; we would have anticipated our history as a people I believe, by a great many years. For, under our old ideas, say, for instance, in the province from which I come, we had not thought Mr. BELL.

whatever of using the tariff as a means of promoting industry. We had, up to 1857, or thereabouts, a simple tariff of 10 per cent, intended to provide for the government of the day the comparatively small sums sufficient for the public affairs of a community living in the comparatively primitive and undeveloped state in which we were then living. We were simply producers of raw material. Our trade was with flie United States to a large extent. We sent them our farm products as far as they would accept them, our fish and our plaster, and we received from them almost every item of manufacture that we used. The manufacture of the simplest form of wooden-ware was unknown in our province. It was not until, by the fortunate circumstance of the United States refusing to continue the operation of the old reciprocity treaty we were forced to enter upon a course of industry which, since that day, we have been pursuing with a certain amount of success. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that the House ought to affirm the resolution which has been tendered by the hon. member for St. Mary's division. At the same time, I suppose we could not expect that to be done on the present occasion. We can scarcely expect the government to have made up its mind to accept that position. We know, on the other hand, that the government has chosen to take this attitude as expressed by the Minister of Finance in the course of his budget speech, they would prefer to regard the position in which they stand and have stood for the past year since the last budget speech was made, as one that they think ought to satisfy the manufacturers of the country. Because, to quote, not with verbal precision, but with fair accuracy, the statement made by the Minister of Finance, they wish to give to the manufacturers the idea that what is uppermost in the mind of tlje government of the day is stability-no change for the better, no change for the worse, no advancement, no retreat. As I understand them they chose to stand by the tariff as they gave it to the country in 1897, with certain small changes that have been made since that time. They choose to regard that as satisfactory for the time, and they are not prepared to meet with acceptance the very strong proposition made by the hon. gentleman from St. Mary's division, because it involves the adoption of a system of extreme protection, high protection. It involves the adoption of protection so high as to be adequate, sufficient to retain for the manufacturers of this country every part of the home market; and it would involve a tariff as high as that which the United States raised against our products. I suppose we cannot expect the government of the day to accept it. But, while I heard with great pleasure the argument made by the hon. member for St. Mary's division, I have additional satisfaction in noting that no attempt has been

made on the government side to rebut or meet his argument. I take it, therefore, that we may assume that there is a practical consensus of opinion in the House on this question of protection. We have not heard a single voice raised in support of the old free trade doctrine. We have not heard a word which would lead any one to believe that the government side of the House is occupied by a party which, only seven years ago declared that protection was a system that contained within itself the germs of destruction for any community that adopted it, that it was a system accursed, injurious, and one under which no community could expect to make progress. They said it could be described as legalized robbery, that its operation was the creation of combines, the creation of barons of wealth and industry on the one hand, and of the poor, degraded classes, the downtrodden classes, on the other. We have not heard lately one word of that language with which the country was familiar for many years. Therefore. Mr. Speaker, I suppose we may fairly assume that the party now occupying the government side of the House has abandoned their old position, and that we will hear nothing more of it in the future, either in this House or in the [DOT] country. That I would look upon as an exceedingly favourable omen to this Dominion, because I am satisfied from what I have seen and know of the conditions in our country and in other countries, in the mother country and in those rival nations which are contending with it for the trade of the world. I have seen, I say, sufficient to make an argument that is practically unanswerable, that under present conditions, and in face of the commercial war that is now being waged the world over by every nation that aims at attaining a leading position, there is one weapon that must be in every one's armoury, and that weapon is protection. Without the control and maintenance of the home market, no country can hope to attain to anything like success.

After fifty years, and those fifty years representing the dominance of a school which did not permit a public man to dare to question the correctness of the free trade theory, Great Britain, under the leadership of her foremost statesman, is at this moment apparently making up her mind that Imposition is in danger of being destroyed permanently if she stands by it. We see the evidence in that startling, that epochmaking speech delivered by the secretary for the colonies after his return from South Africa, a speech which startled every one as might a thunderclap coming from the clear sky, a speech that is being talked over, reasoned about, and the prediction is freely made now that within the course of two or three months, with such education as could be given by a reasonable campaign of education, the Right Hon. Mr. Chamberlain might hope to secure the support of the majority of the electors of Great Britain. That goes to show that facts are being forced upon the minds of tfie people of Great Britain that an adherence to the old doctrine of free trade means an inevitable decline and loss of their markets, the loss of their pre-eminence. Therefore if that be the case, if Great Britain is to be driven from the position which for fifty years she has held with such apparent triumphant success, driven to abandon the doctrine of free trade and to range herself with the other nations of the world under the banner of protection, then I say that the last example which can be quoted by any supporter of the free trade doctrine will be removed. Look over the world where you will, you will find that the secret of success for a country which aspires $>

eminence in industrial pursuits and all that tends to greatness in national life, is to use the weapons of commercial war in order to maintain the existence and maintain the progress which that nation may have realized. It is too late to-night, and it is not necessary, in view of the facts that arguments are not Being made at all from the government side of the House, to enter upon an argument in support of the protectionist theory. There can be no question that Great Britain achieved her success, and her position from which she could start out triumphantly upon a free trade course, by a system of protection of the most extreme character continuing for many centuries. There can be no question that by her protective system she displaced the Dutch, who up to that time had held the leading position in the commerce of the world. There can be no doubt that when France, Germany and the other nations of the world realized that Great Britain had become the great mercantile power of the world, and held a position they would like to occupy, they attacked her position by setting up in their respective domains a protective system which gives them their own market, and from the advantage ground of which they are able to attack Great Britain in the other markets of the world. There can be no question that protection is the only system that can be adopted by any country which wishes to develop in the direction of industrial greatness.

Now I am sure while we are delighted to know that in this country we have great natural advantages, and great agricultural possibilities, and great natural wealth, there is not a gentleman in this House who would deliberately choose for Canada a future in which the people were to be only producers of raw materials, were even to sup'ply wheat or meat, or fish for other countries, to be consumed in the great manufacturing centres by a teeming population gathered there by industrial activity. That is not a future we want to see for Canada. We want to see Canada building upon the basis of all

this natural wealth, of this enormous food supply, of her wonderful fisheries, of her great mass of raw material, her extensive waterways, her sources of coal-we want to see built upon that basis a great industrial community. We want to see her industries developed, we want to see our people, not employed in the humbler, and grosser, and more poorly remunerated vocations which are required in order to supply the raw material for other people, but we want to see them engaged in the most highly developed, the most difficult, the most technical pursuits that are anywhere in the world being pursued by men of whom we think ourselves at least the equals if not the superiors. Therefore it seems to me absolutely essential that if there be any cpgency or power in the case made here today by the hon. member for St. Mary's, we ought either to controvert it or to assent to it. If we cannot controvert it, then I say it is our duty to agree with his proposition, to make it perfectly plain and unmistakable to the people of Canada and to the world generally, that for our part we have chosen that better course which is involved in adopting once for all the policy of protection, of such a character, so far-developed, as to be adequate, sufficient to effect the purpose for which it is intended, namely, to protect the industries of Canada and keep the market of Canada for Canadians.

69811,ca.proc.d.1903-06-17.3.3.39,1903-06-17,3f3a6135-5d1d-4167-ab81-0e1dbb2cd149,ca.m.3785,Mr. GOURLEY.,,SUPPLY-GOVERNMENT TARIFF POLICY.,IT, 1903",,"I understood there is an unwritten rule of parliament that a member should serve three years before he is competent to indulge at any length in the public debates of this House ; and as I was bred in a trade that believes in precedence, I bowed to that rule, and governed myself accordingly. I am free to declare that a policy which would suit England may not be suited to Canada, because this is a new country and we have to meet new conditions, and even if it wrsre wise to have free trade in England, I would argue as a logical conclusion that we ought to have protection on the American continent. to settle the fiscal values of this country, and we cannot be guided by the old world views, which may suit France or Germany or England. 69815,ca.proc.d.1903-06-17.3.3.43,1903-06-17,3f3a6135-5d1d-4167-ab81-0e1dbb2cd149,ca.m.3785,Mr. GOURLEY.,,SUPPLY-GOVERNMENT TARIFF POLICY.,IT, 1903",,"We have adopted in this country a system of free schools; we make

our mechanics educated men; we give them the tastes of scholars and students, and let me ask: are you going to introduce a fiscal system into this country that will give to such educated mechanics the same wages as are paid to the ignorant mechanics of France and Germany and England ? No, you must adopt a policy that is suitable to the conditions of this country. ,Conservative (1867-1942),,Seymour Eugene Gourley,http://www.parl.gc.ca/parlinfo/Files/Parliamentarian.aspx?Item=3f3a6135-5d1d-4167-ab81-0e1dbb2cd149&Language=E&Section=ALL
69816,ca.proc.d.1903-06-17.3.3.44,1903-06-17,3f3a6135-5d1d-4167-ab81-0e1dbb2cd149,ca.m.3785,Mr. GOURLEY.,,SUPPLY-GOVERNMENT TARIFF POLICY.,IT, 1903",,"I am enforcing the principle of protection to our industries, a principle that has been enforced by the most competent and most capable men of the United States. The difficulties we are meeting in Canada to-day were met and overcome years ago in the United States by men like Henry Clay and Daniel Webster. I venture to say that the words of these men have demolished for ever on this continent, any sound argument in support of free trade. Daniel Webster very truly said : Can you compare the educated American [DOT] artisan to the ignorant dunce and the besotted workmen of some manufacturing towns in England, Germany or France. If you cannot do that, then we must adopt on this continent a policy that will suit our conditions and give our workingmen higher wages. I will undertake to say that the mechanics of this country are organizing ; they are getting educated leaders, and if you attempt to give them the small wage of $1.10 or $1.50 a day, you are making a great mistake. We must endeavour to educate the manufacturers of this country up to the point of paying to educated mechanics such wages as will give their families an education suitable to their style of life. Therefore we must have protection for our industries in order that the cheap goods of Germany and England shall be shut out. Our manufacturers, if they are compelled to pay high wages, must get good prices for their goods and be protected from the slaughtered goods of the countries that employ cheap labour. That is a doctrine which these hon. gentlemen do not seem to understand. I tell you that the mechanics of the maritime provinces are holding meetings and discussing this question, and they demand from $2 to $2.50 per day for ordinary mechanics as a minimum wage. When you discuss the question from the standpoint of the educated mechanic, recognizing that every boy and every girl must be educated, and that every home is a home' of refinement, you upset all the arguments drawn from the free trade system of

England, because they are based upon conditions of ignorance and want which I hope will never be present in Canada. You must grapple with this question as the educated men of the United States grappled with it; and when the intelligent and logical people of that country, although originally free traders, became indoctrinated with the idea that a new principle must be applied to the continent of America, they applied it to the United States, as we must apply it to Canada, or we shall ,fail in the race of development. That is the genesis of the whole question of free trade and protection on this continent. Therefore I do not feel overwhelmed when the hon. gentleman referred me to Free Trade England. I ask them to discuss the question from the standpoint of America. The conditions of life on this account are different from those of any country in Europe. We must deal with the matter according to the -conditions as we find them ; and when we find a great commercial nation like the United States, a country more filled with universities and schools, with classical, mathematical and technical education, than almost all the world beside-when we find an astute people like that adopting wholesale the principle of protection, does it not seem a folly for a gentleman like the hon. Minister of Finance, who knows nothing practically about free trade and protection, who knows nothing practically about manufacturing or the conditions of trade, to ask us to accept the policy of free trade ? When he does so he adds neither light nor argument to the subject.

I want to thank the hon. member for Centre Toronto (Mr. Brock) for the splendid address he made. I think it was a splendid augury-I am a bit superstitious to-night- when Quebec joined hands with Ontario in establishing this new policy of protection, and when an hon. gentleman who left the cabinet, and made the most extraordinary sacrifices that a man can make-if you regard the throwing up of a high office for principle as a sacrifice-joined hands with the hon. member for Centre Toronto. I thought it was a splendid illustration of what was to come hereafter, when public men in this country would agree to throw away mere partisanship whenever the interests of the country were at stake. So far as I am concerned-I presume this will fall on very stony hearts opposite-no party will lead me ten minutes when the interests of the country and the interests of my party conflict; but the Conservative party is led so wisely and has such splendid traditions that it is impossible for such a condition of affairs ever to occur.

Hon. WILLIAM ROSS (Victoria, N.S.) Mr. Speaker, I have considerable sympathy with the hon. member for Colchester (Mr. Gourley) who I think has forgotten his eloquence to-night in trying to belittle the

condition of England, the greatest nation on the earth. He is no true Canadian who would attempt to belittle that country, whose ships go to every part of the world, laden with its productions, and carrying civilization to every place where they go, and that under free trade. It is not right to compare the United States with England; but compare any of the old nations of the continent of Europe with England, and you will see that England under free trade outstrips them all in her power and her manufactures. It is a solid fact that there is manufactured in England to-day double the quantity of cotton that is manufactured in the United States.

Wellington long ago. I must say, that, in my opinion, anything quoted from him could not be of much importance to us in this country. The hon. gentleman spoke of Daniel Webster. would I go ? Certainly not to your side of the House. I hope that when the hon. 69825,ca.proc.d.1903-06-17.3.3.53,1903-06-17,4e01e3c6-73dc-40cf-8a42-e6156318db32,ca.m.3973,Mr. OSLER.,,SUPPLY-GOVERNMENT TARIFF POLICY.,IT, 1903",,"We must have protection if we are going to be anything more than an agricultural country. Unless we have large factories, our brightest young men the best sons of our farmers, who want to go to the cities in order to find an outlet for their energies will, if we have not manufacturing industries, go to the States.

The other question is the question of transportation. Granted protection, it follows as a matter of necessity that we must carry our goods to the market for those goods. We are preparing to expend, and are expending, large sums of money in improving our transportation facilities. I think the hon. member who proposed this resolution probably forgot that we have the promise of the government that the transportation question shall be put in the hands of a very able, a first class commission, and the question is to be solved without any delay and without any doubt. BOUDEN (Halifax).,Leader of the Official Opposition,SUPPLY-GOVERNMENT TARIFF POLICY.,IT, 1903",,"Before the question is put, I wish to say a few words, and 1 promise the House 1 shall not detain them more than a few minutes. The resolution proposed by the hon. member for St. Mary's division (Hon. Mr. Tarte) while somewhat more elaborate in its terms, is to all intents and purposes the same in purport as that proposed to the House by myself during the present session, and the same in purport as those 1 had the honour to propose during last session, and the session of 1901. The hon. member for St. Mary's has supported this resolution with a very able and very exhaustive speech, and he has given to the House and the country two object lessons at least in connection with this matter. In the first place, he has taken the ground that the agricultural interest of this country is of greater importance to the country as a whole than any other, and he has directed the attention of the House to the result fipon the agricultural industry of Great Britain of the policy of free trade which has been maintained there for the last fifty years. He has pointed out-or if he did not, lie might have done so-how much more fatal to the agricultural industry of this country a policy of free trade would be than to the same industry in the mother country. Because while Great Britain has been mainly a manufacturing country, she did have agricultural resources to a very considerable extent, and formerly those resources were developed under different conditions to such an extent that they were almost of as much importance as the manufacturing industry. The hon. gentleman might have shown, as I have said, that if free trade is ruinous to agriculture in Great Britain it would be infinitely more runious to this country. We are competitors with the United States in the sale of agricultural products in the markets of Europe. And we must always be so. The United States may possibly, as years roll on, find more and more a home market for their agricultural products, but they must always to some extent, look to Europe. Our competition with the United States is carried on under very peculiar conditions. Not only are the manufacturing industries of that country coming under the control of great trusts and combines, but the agricultural industry -or, at least the agricultural output-of the United States is largely coming under the control of great combines which control prices not only in the United States but throughout the world's markets. Look at the condition with regard to the iron industry to-day. The United States, with its enormous output of iron and steel controls through its combines, the output for export from Germany as well, and, in that

Then, the hon. gentleman pointed out the results of a protective policy in the United States upon the manufacturing industries of that country. He pointed out that in many manufacturing industi'ies the United States had not only overtaken but surpassed the mother country. And, in answer to my hon. friend from Victoria, N.S. (Hon. Mr. Ross), I would point out that this question is assuming very important dimensions in the mother country, and that every day is adding to the acuteness of the situation as bringing more and more attention to the question whether free trade shall be maintained in Great Britain or whether England shall attempt to stem the torrent of competition throughout the world by some measure of protection to her industries.

Now I would call the policy which the hon. gentleman has advocated to-night, and which we on this side have advocated in the past, a policy of national commercial self-defence for Canada. That is what it is, nothing more and nothing less. We remember in the old days of fifty years ago, when the volunteer movement was first agitated in Great Britain, the motto of the English volunteer was ' Defence not defiance.' So it is in commercial matters in Canada to-day. We are face to face with high tariffs, with policies of protection prevailing in every country in the world ; and the question is whether we shall adopt in Canada that policy which is so well outlined in the resolution of my hon. friend for St. Mary's, and which I think we might well call a policy of national commercial selfdefence for Canada. If we do not adopt it, where are we to stand ? Are we to stand alone in the world in allowing our markets to be open to foreign competition to such an extent that our own industries will be
destroyed ? Outside of England there is nothing like our position among all the nations of the world.

I think, Mr. Speaker, that the government might well have made some pronouncement to-night. It is true that the Minister of Finance made a pronouncement earlier in the session, and if I might be permitted briefly to refer to it, it amounts to this, that our industries are so prosperous in Canada, our warehouses so full and overflowing, that there is not the slightest need for a revision of the tariff. Well, I think some incidents that have taken place during the past few months have perhaps taken away something of the weight which the utterances of the Minister of Finance possessed at the time. The hon. gentleman told us that no capitalist was deterred from investing money in Canada by reason of the uncertainty of the fiscal policy of the government. I do not know whether the Minister of Finance would be so confident about that to-day, and I am not sure that if he were very frank with the House, he would jot be able to tell us that certain assurances have been required, at least, whether they have been given or not, before further capital will be invested in some of the great industries in Canada which hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House are most anxious to maintain in this country. Now let us look for a moment at the resolution of my hon. friend from St. Mary's. He declares :

That it is the bounden and imperative duty of the government to revise and readjust, without any further delay, the present tariff in such a manner as to leave no doubt as to the determination of the Canadian people to adopt and maintain a fiscal policy adequately and firmly protective of the large national interests at stake.
Now that is a pretty definite statement, it seems to me. It may be characterized by the Minister of Finance as being vague.

I do not know whether he would ask his followers to vote it down because it is too vague, or because it is inopportune, or on what other ground. But I venture to say that no hon. gentleman on the other side of the House can stand up in his place and give any adequate reason why there should not be a declared and pronounced policy in Canada to the effect stated in the resolution. At least, no hon. gentleman on the other side of the House has seen fit to do so, if I may put aside for a moment the somewhat general utterances of the hon. member for Victoria (Hon. Mr. Ross), whose courage and sincerity, and whose convictions, I am sure, we all admire. But if my hon. friend the Minister of Finance and the government think that by sitting silent and refusing to discuss these motions, they are going to better their position in the country, I am inclined to think they will find themselves somewhat mistaken. They will have to answer these matters sooner or later in the end, and there will come a time when

they cannot sit dumb in their seats and say nothing about motions of this kind proposed to the House. That time may not be very far off. What are the reasons, what are the grounds, advanced in the resolution of my hon. friend ?

To assure the permanency and the further progress of the existing industries, as well as the creation of many new ones that only -wait the proper policy to spring up ; to inspire greater confidence in Canadian, British and foreign capital seeking investment in our own country.

I ask hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House whether we cannot look around Canada to-day and observe in the condition of certain industries the best possible ground for my hon. friend from St. Mary's proposing this resolution to the House, and supporting it by the arguments we have heard ? Then he proceeds :

To secure for the farmers now tilling our soil and those that we invite to share the blessings of our institutions and the wealth that Providence has placed at our disposal, the full advantage of a prosperous home market.

My hon. friend has put his grounds with regard to that so well that it is not necessary for me to amplify them, except possibly by one illustration. Would it be better or worse for the farmers of this country if we were to throw down our tariff walls, and if the great industries which are being built up, and which should be built up in the future, were built up in the United States of America ? Would it be better or worse for Canada that that should happen ? The articles which are required in Canada for use by our workingmen and by our farmers, are articles that we can manufacture in Canada ; and will anv hon. gentleman in this House, in his sane moments, say that it is not better for Canada to have the cities and centres of industry in our own country, and to supply these articles for our own people, by our own workmen, by means of our own capital? Well, that is what my hon. friend from St. Mary's proposes by this resolution, and bv the reasons which I have just adduced. The hon. gentleman points out that so far as the farmers are concerned it is better for them to have the centres of industry in our own country, because the creation of these centres of industry affords to the people a prosperous home market. Then he goes on further and he advances another reason :
To comply with the legitimate desire of the working classes to see their labour rewarded by fair and uninterrupted wages, and by comfort in their families.

That is a ground which has been taken before in this House, a ground which I myself have taken, when I pointed out, during previous sessions, the fact that the conditions of life in Canada among the labouring classes are different from those which prevail in many countries whose

goods enter into competition with our own. We know that the workmen of the continent of Europe and of some of the Southern states of the neighbouring republic do not live under the same conditions, do not have the same standard of living as that to which the people of our own country are accustomed. We cannot expect that the manufacturing industries of this country can be maintained unless they are protected by a tariff which is as much for the advantage of the workingmen who are employed in our factories and industries as it is for the advantage of the man who puts capital into these industries.
To render impossible the slaughtering ot our markets by the products of foreign industries, of foreign combines, of foreign agriculture and of cheap labour countries.

This is carrying out the idea so many times advanced in this House, that while we can deal with combines in Canada by our own legislation-and we have attempted to deal with them by legislation introduced by this government-legislation of that kind is only useful against foreign combines so long as we have an adequate protective tariff, because when you once throw down the tariff wall you admit the combine to do in Canada exactly what it is doing iu the United States, or in any other country. Yon can only guard adequately against the influence of foreign combines by giving proper protection to your home industries, and unless you do that, you will have the industries of this country, and what is more, the consumers of this country, placed at the mercy of such combines, whose effects are well known, and have been commented upon over and over again by writers on political economy in the United States of America. Then my hon. friend continues :
To bring about a quicker development and a more rapid expansion of our vast resources.
I will not pause to discuss that point. And as his last reason :
To promote closer commercial relations between the different provinces of the Dominion and between this Dominion and the mother country.
Then, in regard to that and especially iu regard to that, my hon. friend has concluded his resolution in these words :

And also to carry out an energetic transportation policy which will give to our merchandise and products of all kinds commodious, quick and cheap access to the markets of our country and to those of foreign nations trading with us.

There is this peculiarity in our situation that the portion of Canada which is more particularly inhabited is what might be called relatively a narrow strip lying for 4.000 miles alongside of tbe United States of America, and while that gives an opportunity to the merchants and manufacturers of the United States to seek Canadian markets it is very difficult for the people in the east and the people in the west of

I was not present, but I am informed that that deputation, speaking on behalf of the working classes, appealed to this government not to increase the tariff, because they were satisfied that an increase would not be for the benefit of the labouring classes. The farmers !-why, Sir, they have been paying off their mortgages. I was talking to-night to a respected member of this House belonging to the province of Ontario, and he told me that it was within his knowledge that farmers who not many years ago were obliged to borrow money, were not only paying off their mortgages, but were bringing in money and asking for investments for it. Bet me add that Avhile great changes have been made by the Liberal party in the tariff, Avhile hundreds of items have been reduced, and large and important items, it so happens that in this particular class of items, except in three or four cases, the duties on agricultural products are the same to-day as they were under the national policy. The only difference is that under the national policy the farmers were not so prosperous as they are to-day under a Liberal government. That is the happy condition with respect to the farmers. With respect to capital, my hon. friend the leader of the opposition speaks of the uncertainty which

prevents an investment of capital. My hon. friend cannot be serious. Does be not know that during the seven years of the Liberal administration, the 'Canada Gazette' and the provincial gazettes, have absolutely groaned with notices of new companies and new promotion schemes for the investment of capital in Canada ? I venture to say that during the seven years of the Liberal administration, there has been more capital invested in manufacturing industries in Canada than in any fourteen years in the previous history of the country. I am not speaking of things which are not of common knowledge. Any gentleman who looks at the newspapers, knows that in every part of this country there has been an enormous development of industry. Whether you go to the labourer, the manufacturer, the farmer, or the business man, there is the universal story of widespread industry and prosperity. It cannot be universal as respects every individual, because in any time of prosperity, you will find certain sections or individuals who are not as prosperous as we would like them to be ; but speaking in the large, as respects the country generally, it is not too much to say that during the whole previous history of the Dominion of Canada the country never prospered as it lies prospered in the seven years under the administration of the government of Sir Wilfrid Laurier.
